analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on multinational corporations' offshore profits brought home to 5.25% for one year.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted a Republican sponsor and 45 cosponsors but never received a committee vote, dying in the House Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the tax rules of the time, American companies did not owe U.S. tax on profits earned by their foreign subsidiaries until those profits were paid back to the U.S. parent company. This bill would have let a company elect, for a single year, to pay a 5.25% tax on dividends it brought home above its recent historical average, instead of the roughly 35% corporate rate that normally applied. It also cut by 85% the foreign tax credits those companies could claim on the money they brought home. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. multinational corporations with large piles of accumulated offshore profits. For one year, they could repatriate the excess at a 5.25% rate instead of the ordinary corporate rate, converting profits that had been parked abroad at a fraction of the normal U.S. tax cost. Their shareholders would benefit through the tax savings and whatever the companies did with the cash.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposed a 5.25% 'toll tax' on an electing company's excess dividends from its controlled foreign corporations, imposed in lieu of the normal individual or corporate income tax on those amounts.
The bill cut the foreign tax credits a company could claim on the repatriated amount by 85%, which was part of how the low 5.25% effective rate was structured.

Supporters' stated purpose was 'to encourage investing of foreign earnings within the United States for productive business purposes' — the idea that a one-time low rate would draw offshore cash back home.

The election applied to all of a company's controlled foreign corporations and, for affiliated groups, was made by the common parent, letting large corporate groups bring the full volume of their offshore earnings under the low rate.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally. Revenue that would normally have been collected at the full corporate rate on those repatriated profits would instead be collected at 5.25%. Nothing in the bill required companies to use the money for hiring, investment, or any specific purpose.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no requirement that repatriated cash be used for hiring, investment, or wages — a company could elect the low rate and spend the money on anything, including buying back its own stock, while the Treasury collected far less than the normal corporate rate would have raised.

The structure rewards companies for having kept profits offshore: the bigger the excess over their historical dividend average, the more they gained, which would pressure future Congresses to offer similar holidays.

Even at 5.25%, the tax was a real cost to the companies electing it, and supporters would argue the bill was a one-year, self-limiting window rather than a permanent rate cut — the strongest good-faith defense is that some revenue and some domestic investment is better than none on money that might have stayed offshore indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a large, targeted tax break to a specific set of companies without any strings on how the money was used. The upside — some offshore cash returning home and some revenue collected on money that might otherwise owe nothing — is real but speculative; the cost — a large reduction in tax on profits those companies had earned and deferred for years — was certain. The absence of any use-of-proceeds requirement meant the public benefit depended entirely on companies choosing to invest rather than pay shareholders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the Congress ended in early 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English introduced the bill on February 13, 2003, joined by Reps. Dreier, Brady of Texas, and Dunn as original cosponsors, with the stated goal of encouraging investment of foreign earnings in the United States.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
That was the bill's final action: it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died in committee when the 108th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers were spared the cost of a large one-year tax break for multinationals' offshore profits, and the companies that would have benefited gained nothing from this particular bill. The general corporate and Treasury-hawk side of the argument won by default, since the committee simply never acted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the bill's corporate backers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Homeland Investment Act and recruited 45 cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. David Dreier, Kevin Brady, and Jennifer Dunn
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 45 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a solid bloc of Republican support in the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; its chair never scheduled the bill for action
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican — 45 of them alongside the Republican sponsor — and no Democratic support or recorded opposition appears in the record; the bill's fate was decided quietly in committee rather than by a vote.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with large offshore earnings
industries.note: The bill would have let these companies bring accumulated foreign profits home at 5.25% instead of the roughly 35% corporate rate, a windfall worth billions depending on how much cash they repatriated. The tax savings come out of federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers would otherwise fund, and no provision tied the money to jobs or investment.

industries.industry: Purely domestic companies without foreign subsidiaries
industries.note: These companies would have gotten no benefit from the bill while their multinational competitors received a large tax cut on repatriated profits, putting them at a relative disadvantage in capital and acquisition markets.
